papers.abstract: Platinum-based chemotherapy remains a standard-of-care treatment for non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet its efficacy is influenced by multiple factors, such as the functionality of DNA damage response pathways. DNA-damaging agents, like cisplatin, contribute to the generation of an "inflamed" tumor microenvironment (TME), which in turn correlates with an active antitumor immune response. MicroRNAs (miRNAs), a family of small, non-coding RNAs, have emerged as critical post-transcriptional regulators of gene expression, playing vital roles in modulating DNA Damage Repair (DDR) pathways and sensitivity to cisplatin. Their functional involvement in these mechanisms underscores their potential as diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers in lung cancer. In this study, we investigated the diagnostic and prognostic value of a previously validated six-miRNA signature (hsa-miR-26a, hsa-miR-29c, hsa-miR-34a, hsa-miR-30-5p, hsa-miR-30e-3p and hsa-miR-497) in paired tumor and healthy tissue samples from surgically treated NSCLC patients (n = 76), who later received platinum-based therapy. To explore the translational applicability of this signature, we also compared miRNA expression levels between matched tumor tissue and plasma samples (n = 36). We further examined the presence of an "inflamed" TME and its association with the miRNA signature by examining the mRNA levels of TIGIT, CD8A, FOXP3, CXCL10 and PD-L1, and performing correlation analysis. All selected miRNAs were significantly downregulated in NSCLC tumor tissue compared to healthy samples. Moreover, miRNA expression was differentially regulated in plasma samples, supporting their potential clinical relevance as minimally invasive biomarkers. The complete six-miRNA signature demonstrated good discriminatory ability between tumor and matched non-malignant tissue (AUC = 0.786, 95% CI: 0.713-0.860; p < 0.001), with 72% sensitivity and 77.3% specificity. A significant correlation with relapse-free survival (RFS) (p = 0.039) was also observed. Distinct immune-related transcriptional alterations were observed in tumor tissue, including increased expression of immune checkpoint-associated genes (TIGIT and PD-L1) and reduced CD8A expression. Tumor PD-L1 expression showed modest positive correlations with miR-26a (p = 0.046) and miR-30e-3p (p = 0.031). Our findings underscore the potential value of this novel six-miRNA signature both as a prognostic and diagnostic biomarker in NSCLC. Its correlation with immune microenvironment characteristics supports its relevance in guiding personalized therapeutic strategies. This signature warrants further clinical validation and may serve as a valuable tool for patient stratification and outcome prediction for patients treated with platinum-based chemotherapy.

papers.abstract: PM is a locally aggressive tumor associated with asbestos exposure. Despite legislative efforts to regulate asbestos use, its incidence continues to rise in some parts of the world. Chemotherapy and immunotherapy have improved survival in PM patients, but overall survival remains poor. MTAP loss is frequent in PM and may influence tumor behavior, resulting in a poorer prognosis. MTAP-deficient tumors exhibit unique metabolic vulnerabilities that have stimulated the development of targeted therapeutic strategies in recent years with promising results. The aim of this review is to analyze the prognostic and predictive value of MTAP in PM patients, as well as the outcomes of drugs with potential activity against this target.

papers.abstract: Background: Maximal safe resection remains the cornerstone of glioma surgery, particularly in eloquent regions where oncologic gain must be balanced against functional preservation. While 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA) fluorescence-guided surgery improves extent of resection in high-grade gliomas under general anesthesia, its role during awake craniotomy (AC) remains underdeveloped. We aimed to evaluate the oncologic and functional outcomes of 5-ALA-guided tumor resection during AC. Methods: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception to February 2026 for studies reporting original data on AC using 5-ALA following PRISMA guidelines. Results: Across ten studies comprising 108 patients, fluorescence positivity was 79.2% in high-grade gliomas (Grade III-IV) and 24.1% in low-grade gliomas (Grade II), among the 83 patients with both grade and fluorescence data available (grade was not reported for 19 patients in one case series, and 6 patients in one cohort study did not receive 5-ALA and were excluded from grade- and fluorescence-stratified analyses). Gross total resection was achieved in 62.2% of patients with evaluable extent-of-resection data (56.5% of the full cohort), reaching 66.7% in the largest comparative cohort. Transient aphasia occurred in 32.6% of evaluable patients, while permanent aphasia and persistent hemiparesis were observed in 14.6% and 16.9%, respectively. In multiple studies, resection was intentionally halted despite persistent fluorescence when functional mapping identified an eloquent cortex, underscoring that mapping remained the decisive determinant of surgical boundaries. No study reported conversion to general anesthesia. Conclusions: 5-ALA-guided resection during AC appears feasible and clinically useful, particularly for high-grade gliomas in eloquent regions. Permanent neurological morbidity was observed in a minority of patients, within a range broadly consistent with awake glioma surgery generally, but the absence of a non-5-ALA comparator group means that functional safety relative to awake mapping alone cannot yet be established with confidence. Across the available literature, 5-ALA consistently enhances intraoperative tumor visualization, supports identification of residual fluorescent disease, and integrates well with cortical and subcortical mapping without clear evidence of increased permanent neurological morbidity. Although functional mapping remains the decisive determinant of the final resection boundary, the available evidence supports 5-ALA as a valuable complementary adjunct in onco-functional glioma surgery.

papers.abstract: Giant keratinocyte carcinomas, comprising basal cell carcinoma (BCC) and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) with a maximum diameter ≥ 5 cm, pose substantial clinical challenges. This structured narrative review distinguishes giant-specific findings from contextual evidence in advanced or high-risk disease. The synthesis uses a retained bibliography assembled from searches described in earlier drafts as covering PubMed/MEDLINE and PubMed Central from January 2015 to March 2026, supplemented by citation and guideline searching and a focused update reported through 4 September 2026. A record-level search and screening log is unavailable; historical selection counts cannot be independently reconstructed. The review protocol was not registered, and exhaustive coverage or full PRISMA compliance is not claimed. Sources were classified by design and directness, with descriptive consideration of methodological limitations. The retained set contains 51 sources: nine containing direct giant-specific clinical evidence and 42 providing contextual evidence. Direct evidence consists principally of case reports, retrospective or comparative studies and a giant-cSCC literature synthesis. It links giant BCC with prolonged lesion duration, ulceration, deeper invasion and reconstructive burden. Giant-cSCC outcomes vary substantially between reported series. Evidence for Hedgehog-pathway inhibition, PD-1 blockade and most molecular mechanisms derives mainly from conventional or advanced disease. Management requires multidisciplinary assessment integrating size, pathological risk, resectability and patient factors. Giant-specific molecular and therapeutic evidence remains limited, and contextual treatment effects should not be interpreted as effects established specifically in tumours ≥ 5 cm.

papers.abstract: CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has transformed the treatment of relapsed/refractory large B-cell lymphoma (r/r LBCL), yet primary resistance and relapse remain common. We evaluated how recent clinical and translational evidence refines established resistance frameworks and which knowledge gaps prevent the relative contribution of individual mechanisms from being determined. We conducted a structured narrative review of 14 selected clinical and translational studies addressing tumor-, product-, host-, and microenvironment-related dimensions of treatment failure, synthesized across four interpretive domains and compared with nine previous reviews. Durable benefit was associated with favorable tumor and immune transcriptional programs and greater CAR T-cell fitness, expansion, or persistence. Treatment failure was associated with tumor-intrinsic resistance programs, exhausted T-cell states, systemic inflammatory signals, and suppressive tumor-microenvironment features, including PD-L1-expressing macrophages. Antigen escape remained relevant, but incomplete serial CD19 assessment precluded conclusions about its relative contribution. Comparison with earlier reviews showed continuity rather than replacement, with LBCL-focused evidence adding biological resolution. Resistance and relapse after CD19 CAR T-cell therapy in LBCL are multifactorial. Prospective longitudinal studies integrating tumor tissue, apheresis and manufactured products, peripheral blood, and matched relapse samples are needed to validate predictive biomarkers and guide rational treatment strategies.

papers.abstract: Metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has historically been managed with systemic therapy, and local therapies have, in general, been avoided in the absence of symptoms directly related to a specific metastasis. Even if a specific site of disease, such as a local recurrence, had the potential to cause symptoms in the future, there was a bias against prophylactic palliation. It was well-established that most patients die of systemic progression. This approach is now under pressure from four directions. Retrospective case series have reported survival durations longer than anticipated in highly selected patients with low-volume, single-organ disease. A randomized phase II trial reported that metastasis-directed therapy prolonged progression-free survival. Biologic data indicate that the site of metastatic relapse is encoded in gene expression profiles already present in the primary tumor. Second-line systemic therapy has become substantially more effective, which lengthens the interval over which control of an untreated metastasis may become clinically important. We trace the oligometastatic concept from the 1995 Hellman and Weichselbaum hypothesis to the 2026 OligoPanc consensus definition of up to three lesions confined to a single organ, examine the criteria proposed for patient selection, summarize the surgical and ablative radiotherapy literature, and consider the trials that will determine whether this is a treatable disease state or a favorable prognostic phenotype. We conclude that induction systemic therapy, followed by response assessment that weighs the absence of disease progression, Carbohydrate Antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) kinetics, and performance status, is a defensible route to local therapy directed at the metastases and the primary tumor, and warrants prospective study.

papers.abstract: Reliable and reproducible imaging-response assessment is essential for endpoint evaluation in glioblastoma clinical trials. The Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology (RANO) criteria provide a rule-based framework for standardisation, but their implementation can still yield variable outputs between readers and across timepoints and trial sites. This partly reflects differences in lesion definition, measurement geometry, longitudinal tracking, and new-lesion adjudication. We externally evaluated an automated pipeline for auditable, RANO 2.0-aligned imaging-only response assessment using pre-existing segmentation masks. This retrospective feasibility and pilot evaluation used longitudinal glioblastoma magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies from the public single-centre LUMIERE dataset. Dataset-provided tumour segmentation masks were retained unchanged. An expert neuroradiologist visually reviewed the masks against the corresponding MRI images, and timepoints with segmentations clearly non-representative of tumour tissue were excluded. Deterministic rule-based processing performed lesion definition, admissibility-filtered measurement extraction, longitudinal tracking, new-lesion detection, and provisional response classification. Expert RANO imaging annotations and bidimensional measurements served as comparators rather than complete clinical RANO 2.0 adjudications. Analyses assessed agreement in the sum of products of diameters (SPD), longitudinal burden change, response classification, progression timing, new-lesion agreement, and failure modes, with patient-level clustered bootstrap resampling. Visual segmentation quality control excluded 57 timepoints across 42 patients, leaving 542 evaluable timepoints, including 506 matched to expert annotations. Across 84 expert-measured timepoints from 47 patients, the constrained maximum product of perpendicular diameters (Max-PPD-c) correlated with expert SPD (Pearson r = 0.753; Spearman ρ = 0.861), although the concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) was 0.680 and the median absolute percentage difference was 36.8%. Overall, 73.8% of measurements were within ±50% of expert SPD. Across 31 consecutive pairs from 17 patients, correlations for longitudinal percentage change were r = 0.715 and ρ = 0.874. Per-timepoint four-class response agreement was 48.1% (κ = 0.173), whereas final-timepoint binary progressive disease (PD) agreement was 76.0%. Among patients with PD by both methods, the pipeline assigned PD earlier more often than later, although the median timing difference was 0.0 weeks and the paired comparison was not statistically significant (p = 0.068). New-lesion detection had a positive predictive value (PPV) of 22.3% and negative predictive value (NPV) of 89.0%. Conservative patient-level later-positivity estimates were 10.8% within 12 weeks and 27.0% within 24 weeks, without same-lesion verification. This study supports the value of a deterministic pipeline for standardising imaging-derived response outputs in glioblastoma clinical trials. Future work will focus on prospective multi-institutional validation incorporating clinical variables, non-enhancing disease assessment, and adjudicated outcomes.

papers.abstract: Renal cancer is a fatal disease and ranks among the 14 common cancers in the latest WHO ranking. Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) prediction not only diagnoses the disease at early stages but also prevents patients from suffering pain and eventual death. This study aimed to construct and validate a model that predicts renal cancer using machine learning (ML) classifiers. Feature engineering techniques were used to refine the dataset, such as interaction feature generation, which categorizes the features according to values such as BMI, eGFR, and radiographic size. Binary clinical risk flags identify clinical risks according to the feature values, and correlation pruning removes the common and correlated features among various features. Three public datasets were collected, and the performance of seven machine learning classifiers was evaluated using the proposed model. The evaluation parameters included accuracy, precision, recall/sensitivity, specificity, F1 score, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC). An Explainable AI method was used to visualize the importance of the model characteristics. Among all the algorithms, the Multilevel Perceptron (MLP) algorithm fits best for the prediction of renal cancer with 98%, 96%, and 100% accuracy, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAPs) are used to visualize the importance of all model features. The proposed model provides an efficient method and shorter computation time to predict renal cancer using clinical features.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: In recent years, the number of cancer survivors has increased. Psychological difficulties or disorders are frequent during survivorship (e.g., fear of cancer recurrence, anxiety, depression, and insomnia). Various interventions have been developed to address survivors' specific psychosocial needs. This rapid scoping review aimed to define the interventions that have been developed for adult cancer survivors by describing (1) the type of intervention, (2) their measured psychosocial outcome variables, and (3) participants' main characteristics. Methods: PubMed was searched for articles published between 2020 and 2025. The search strategy combined terms related to cancer survivorship, psychosocial outcomes, and interventions. Titles and abstracts were screened, and data were extracted using a structured form specifying study type, population, intervention, and outcome characteristics. PRISMA-ScR guidelines were followed. Results: Out of 1743 screened studies, 80 were included (67 studies, 13 systematic reviews/meta-analyses), representing approximately 7880 cancer survivors (from the n = 67). Nearly 45% of included studies were conducted in the United States, and most interventions were developed for breast cancer survivors (38.8%) or included a majority of female participants. Physical activity (22.39%), psychoeducation (17.9%), and cognitive behavioural therapy (16.4%) were the most common intervention types. About a third incorporated eHealth or telehealth. Two-thirds of studies (65.7%) reported predominantly positive effects on psychosocial outcomes. Few interventions included cultural adaptations and targeted minority or socioeconomically disadvantaged populations. Conclusions: Most interventions for cancer survivors targeted breast cancer, female survivors in high-income countries. Developing and implementing culturally adapted and cost-efficient interventions, particularly for underrepresented survivor groups, remains a priority for future research and implementation.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Distant metastasis to the infratemporal fossa (ITF) is rare and can mimic primary skull-base tumors. We systematically reviewed reported distant ITF metastases. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 (PROSPERO CRD420261422546), PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched through 12 June 2026, for reports of ITF metastasis from a distant primary tumor; direct extension from adjacent tumors was excluded. Data were summarized descriptively, and reports were appraised with the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Case Reports. Results: Seventeen reports (17 patients) were included (median age 59 years). The lung was the most frequent primary site (n = 4), followed by the kidney, colorectum, and thyroid (n = 3 each); adenocarcinoma was the most common histology (n = 7). Facial pain (n = 9) and numbness (n = 6) predominated. Bone destruction was reported in 12 patients, and the maxillary sinus (n = 7), orbit (n = 6), pterygopalatine fossa (n = 5), middle cranial fossa (n = 5), and cavernous sinus (n = 4) were involved. The median reported interval to ITF metastasis was 36 months; 11 metastases were metachronous, and 11 patients had other metastatic disease during the reported course. Five patients underwent regional resection or debulking; radiotherapy was reported in eight, radioiodine in three, and systemic drug treatment in nine. At last follow-up, 11 patients were alive, four had died, and status was unknown in two. Conclusions: Distant ITF metastases may present with facial pain and cranial neuropathies. Prognosis is insufficiently characterized, and management should be individualized within a multidisciplinary team. The evidence is limited to case reports with incomplete reporting. No external funding was received.

papers.abstract: Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy worldwide and remains a major cause of cancer-related mortality among women. Despite advances in screening, molecular classification, and systemic therapies, treatment of advanced and metastatic disease remains challenging because of tumor heterogeneity, multidrug resistance, systemic toxicity, limited drug selectivity, and inadequate penetration into the tumor microenvironment. This review aims to critically evaluate advanced drug delivery systems (DDSs) for breast cancer therapy, emphasizing the relationship between carrier design, tumor biology, therapeutic performance, and clinical translation. The recent literature on DDSs for breast cancer treatment was comprehensively reviewed, covering liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles and micelles, dendrimers, nanogels, lipid- and inorganic-based nanoparticles, extracellular vesicles, biomimetic platforms, and stimuli-responsive systems. Particular attention was given to active and passive targeting, controlled drug release, strategies for overcoming multidrug resistance and biological barriers, and combination approaches integrating chemotherapy with immunotherapy, gene therapy, and phototherapy. Clinically approved and clinical-stage nanomedicines were also considered. Advanced DDSs can improve drug stability, pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, tumor accumulation, cellular uptake, and controlled release, potentially enhancing therapeutic efficacy while reducing systemic toxicity. Targeted, biomimetic, and stimuli-responsive platforms provide additional opportunities to address tumor heterogeneity, the tumor microenvironment, and therapeutic resistance. Several DDS-based nanomedicines have reached clinical use or advanced clinical development, demonstrating their translational potential. However, manufacturing scalability, reproducibility, long-term safety, regulatory requirements, and patient heterogeneity remain important barriers. Advanced DDSs represent promising tools for improving the precision and efficacy of breast cancer treatment. Future progress will require biologically informed carrier design, reproducible manufacturing, rigorous clinical validation, and patient stratification. Integrating nanomedicine with precision oncology may accelerate the clinical translation of next-generation DDSs and support more effective personalized therapeutic strategies.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Burkitt lymphoma (BL) is an aggressive germinal center B-cell (gcBC) malignancy driven by MYC deregulation and cooperating molecular alterations. A mouse model combining constitutive MYC and PI3K activity in gcBC closely recapitulates key features of human BL, but its epigenetic similarity to the human disease has not been investigated in detail. Here, we compared genome-wide DNA methylation patterns between human sporadic EBV-negative BL and this murine model. Methods: DNA methylation profiles of 37 human BL samples and 20 gcBC controls were compared with those of 8 murine tumors from the MYC/PI3K driven mouse model and 11 murine gcBC controls using Illumina methylation arrays. Differentially methylated CpGs were identified using linear modeling, and chromatin-state enrichment, cross-species gene overlap, protein interaction, and pathway enrichment analyses were performed. Results: BL showed global DNA hypomethylation in both species and distinct methylation profiles from gcBCs. CpGs hypomethylated in BL were enriched at enhancers, whereas hypermethylated CpGs were strongly enriched at poised promoters. We identified 695 genes with shared hypermethylation and 512 with shared hypomethylation between human and murine BL. Restricting the analysis to regulatory regions identified 86 genes consistently hypomethylated in both species. These genes were significantly enriched for regulation of intracellular signal transduction and sphingolipid signaling. Included are regulators of GTPase and kinase signaling, such as GNA13, RASA3, RASAL1, SPRED2, PIK3R2, PRKCA, PRKCE, and FYN. The conserved set also contained genes with established roles in germinal center B-cell biology, including FOXO1, BACH2, and NR3C1. Conclusions: Human and murine BL share conserved regulatory DNA methylation features, supporting the MYC/PI3K mouse model as a system to study epigenetic mechanisms of BL.

papers.abstract: Background/Hypothesis: Therapeutic resistance and recurrence remain major barriers to durable cancer control because conventional therapies may eliminate proliferating tumor cells while allowing dormant, stem-like, senescence-like, or polyploid populations to persist. This review examines polyploid giant cancer cells (PGCCs) as therapy-tolerant states and evaluates whether their adaptive survival mechanisms create vulnerabilities that could be targeted through ferroptosis-oriented nanomedicine. Methods: We investigated recent evidence (PubMed) linking PGCC persistence with redox buffering, glutathione/GPX4 activity, iron regulation, lipid remodeling, autophagy, mitochondrial adaptation, and metabolic plasticity, in addition to nanomedicine potential to target these pathways. Results and Findings: Emerging studies provide direct proof-of-concept that PGCCs can exhibit ferroptosis susceptibility, while nanomedicine offers potential strategies to improve therapeutic localization and coordinate iron delivery, reactive oxygen species amplification, glutathione depletion, GPX4 inhibition, and combination therapy. However, PGCC-selective nanoparticle efficacy remains largely untested, and important barriers include heterogeneous tumor penetration, off-target toxicity, model limitations, and biomarker uncertainty. Conclusions and Perspective: The specific contribution of this review is to integrate PGCC biology, therapy-tolerant cancer states, ferroptosis, and nanomedicine into a unified framework for targeting residual disease. This perspective is timely as direct evidence of PGCC ferroptosis sensitivity and new characterization of treatment-resistant PGCC states are emerging. By identifying the mechanistic overlap among these fields, this review highlights testable opportunities for eliminating persistent cancer cells that may otherwise contribute to recurrence.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Cutaneous melanoma spreads preferentially through the lymphatic system, and sentinel lymph node status is among the strongest prognostic factors. Whether tumour angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis add prognostic information beyond conventional histopathology has been examined in many immunohistochemical studies, with heterogeneous results. We conducted a systematic review, reported according to PRISMA 2020 and not registered, of blood microvascular density (MVD), lymphatic vessel density (LVD) in the intratumoral and peritumoral compartments, proliferating (Ki-67-positive) lymphatic vessels and lymphatic invasion (LI) as prognostic markers in primary cutaneous melanoma. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE was searched to 10 September 2026, supplemented by a Web of Science export and by citation tracking of the reference meta-analysis by Pastushenko et al. (2014). Twenty-one cutaneous study units (25 reports) and four ocular studies providing indirect evidence were included, and risk of bias was rated with the QUIPS tool. Results: In the reference meta-analysis, peritumoral LVD and LI, but not MVD or intratumoral LVD, were associated with metastasis. The newer cohorts confirmed this pattern and provided adjusted effect sizes: peritumoral LVD predicted disease-free (HR 2.14) and melanoma-specific survival (HR of 2.74; 95% CI 1.31 to 5.73), immunohistochemically detected LI predicted sentinel node metastasis (33% vs. 11% positive nodes) and overall survival, and a Ki-67-positive lymphatic endothelium predicted melanoma-specific mortality (adjusted HR of 2.03; 95% CI 1.33 to 3.10) in 264 patients. Blood MVD and blood endothelial proliferation were not prognostic. Heterogeneity of markers, counting methods and effect measures precluded re-pooling. Conclusions: Peritumoral LVD, LI and proliferating lymphatics are promising adjunct biomarkers for selecting patients for sentinel node biopsy, adjuvant therapy and closer follow-up, pending standardised, digital-pathology-based quantification.

papers.abstract: High tertiary lymphoid structure (TLS) density predicts favorable outcomes in several solid tumors but worse outcomes in bladder cancer, and the basis for this discrepancy is unclear. In this issue, Péricart and colleagues leverage en bloc resection of non-muscle-invasive bladder tumors to show that TLS accumulate without acquiring the features of productive antitumor immunity. The work reframes TLS in this setting as structures for which functional state, not abundance, dictates their contribution to tumor control. See related article by Péricart et al., p. XX.

papers.abstract: Background: Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) has emerged as a potential marker of minimal residual disease (MRD) after resection of colorectal liver metastases (CRLM), but its prognostic value and possible role in guiding postoperative management remain uncertain. This systematic review evaluated the available evidence on ctDNA for predicting recurrence and survival after CRLM resection, with particular attention to perioperative and serial ctDNA measurements and their potential value in guiding adjuvant treatment. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to 21 July 2026 for studies evaluating ctDNA in patients undergoing resection of CRLM. Prospective and retrospective cohort studies and relevant randomized trial sub-studies were eligible. The primary outcome was the association between ctDNA status and recurrence, while secondary outcomes included recurrence-free survival (RFS), disease-free survival (DFS), overall survival (OS), serial ctDNA dynamics, and the potential predictive value of ctDNA for adjuvant chemotherapy. Risk of bias was assessed using the QUIPS tool. Findings were synthesized narratively, with an additional exploratory random-effects meta-analysis of early postoperative tissue-informed ctDNA positivity and RFS/DFS. Unadjusted and adjusted HRs were pooled separately. Results: Twenty-eight studies published between 2018 and 2026 were included, representing 2079 unique patients after accounting for overlapping cohorts. In six studies, postoperative ctDNA positivity was associated with poorer RFS/DFS (pooled unadjusted HR 5.15, 95% CI 3.65-7.27; I2 = 0%). Five studies provided adjusted estimates (pooled HR 4.95, 95% CI 2.45-10.01; I2 = 60.5%). Serial monitoring provided additional prognostic information: persistent ctDNA positivity or conversion from negative to positive during follow-up was associated with poor outcomes, whereas ctDNA clearance was generally associated with a lower risk of recurrence. ctDNA could precede radiological recurrence by approximately 2.5 to >20 months, although detection was less reliable in patients with small-volume pulmonary recurrence. In contrast, the prognostic value of preoperative ctDNA was less consistent and appeared to depend on assay methodology, quantitative ctDNA burden, and previous systemic treatment. Observational studies reported associations between postoperative MRD status and outcomes following adjuvant chemotherapy, but non-randomized treatment allocation and potential time-related bias limit conclusions about treatment benefit. Considerable variation in assay platforms and postoperative sampling schedules remained across studies. Conclusions: Postoperative ctDNA positivity is associated with poorer recurrence-related outcomes after CRLM resection. However, the moderate-to-high risk of bias and differences between studies limit confidence in the evidence. The predictive value of ctDNA for adjuvant chemotherapy benefit remains unproven. Prospective randomized trials are needed to determine whether ctDNA-guided management improves patient outcomes.

papers.abstract: Background: Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) is increasingly implemented for cytoreductive surgery (CRS) combined with hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) for peritoneal surface malignancies (PSM). This systematic review and meta-analysis compared minimally invasive CRS/HIPEC (M-CRS/HIPEC) and open CRS/HIPEC (O-CRS/HIPEC) in terms of perioperative, postoperative, and long-term oncological outcomes. Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted according to PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched for comparative studies of M-CRS/HIPEC versus O-CRS/HIPEC in adult patients. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and RoB 2.0. Pooled relative risks (RR) for dichotomous outcomes and standardized mean differences (SMD) for continuous outcomes were calculated with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the potential influence of disease burden and primary tumor heterogeneity. Results: Twenty-one studies (1 randomized controlled trial and 20 retrospective cohorts) including 1184 patients (452 M-CRS/HIPEC and 732 O-CRS/HIPEC) were analyzed. Operative time did not differ between groups (SMD = 0.195; p = 0.667). Most cytoreductive procedures were comparable, although small bowel resections were less frequent with M-CRS/HIPEC (RR = 0.537; p = 0.018). The minimally invasive approach achieved higher CC0 rates (RR = 1.053; p = 0.045), with lower blood loss (SMD = -1.838; p < 0.001) and fewer transfusions (RR = 0.588; p = 0.002). Postoperative recovery favored M-CRS/HIPEC, with earlier return of bowel function and resumption of oral intake, shorter hospital stay, fewer readmissions, and earlier chemotherapy resumption (all p < 0.05). Overall and major morbidity were reduced, while postoperative mortality and 1-, 3-, and 5-year disease-free and overall survival did not differ significantly between groups. In the disease burden-restricted sensitivity analysis, differences in small bowel resection, CC0 rate, and 90-day readmission were no longer statistically significant, whereas the main perioperative and recovery benefits persisted. No significant differences in DFS or OS were identified in the additional sensitivity analyses at the evaluable time points. Conclusions: This meta-analysis supports a selective, expertise-driven use of M-CRS/HIPEC, offering perioperative and recovery advantages without significant differences in cytoreductive adequacy or long-term outcomes in appropriately selected patients.

papers.abstract: To systematically review the literature on the impact of integrated molecular classification of endometrial cancer on diagnosis, prognostic stratification, and clinical management. A systematic search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and Cochrane Library (January 2013-December 2025), following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. We included original studies, systematic reviews, clinical guidelines, and cost-effectiveness analyses applying TCGA molecular classification or its surrogate classifiers (ProMisE, TransPORTEC). Data were extracted on subtype distribution, survival outcomes, hazard ratios, stage migration, and therapeutic implications. Fifty studies were included. Of these, 13 provided data on molecular subtype distribution (comprising 3527 patients), 8 reported survival outcomes, and 7 reported hazard ratios. The weighted subtype distribution from the 13 studies was as follows: POLEmut 8.9%, MMRd 25.8%, p53abn 16.7%, and NSMP 48.2%. POLEmut was associated with an excellent prognosis (5-year overall survival >95%, hazard ratio 2.0). p53abn was the only independent risk factor for peritoneal (odds ratio 8.54) and vaginal (odds ratio 6.51) recurrence. Molecular classification modified risk group assignment in 6-33% of patients and improved prognostic discrimination of the 2023 FIGO staging system. Therapeutic implications include treatment de-escalation in POLEmut, immunotherapy in MMRd, and intensive chemotherapy in p53abn. Barriers to implementation include access to POLE sequencing and cost-effectiveness. Integrated molecular classification is an essential tool for prognostic stratification and treatment personalization in endometrial cancer. Molecular subtypes demonstrate clearly differentiated prognostic profiles and recurrence patterns, justifying their systematic incorporation into clinical practice and international guidelines.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common primary liver malignancy, and accurate tumour segmentation in contrast-enhanced computed tomography is essential for treatment planning, assessment of ablation margins, and post-treatment evaluation. Existing deep learning methods typically use fixed-intensity CT preprocessing, overlooking the adaptive windowing employed by radiologists to enhance tumour visibility. To address this limitation, we propose BCIW-Net, a boundary-conditioned intensity-windowed network that integrates spatially adaptive and differentiable intensity windowing into the segmentation process as a clinically motivated inductive bias. Methods: The proposed framework first generates complementary soft-tissue and tumour-enhancing intensity representations using differentiable sigmoid-based transformations. A primary encoder-decoder module predicts tumour guidance, boundary probabilities, and pixel-wise error proxy maps, which collectively guide the dynamic estimation of spatially varying window centre and width parameters. The resulting adaptively windowed features are selectively blended with fixed-intensity representations through an error-gated mechanism before final refinement in a secondary encoder-decoder network. A multi-task objective jointly optimises tumour segmentation, boundary prediction, error-proxy estimation, and adaptive window regularisation in an end-to-end manner. Results: Experiments on the primary liver cancer (PLC)-CECT dataset demonstrate that BCIW-Net achieved a mean Dice similarity coefficient of 78.68% and an intersection over union (IoU) of 64.85% across five-fold patient-level cross-validation, outperforming the seven evaluated CNN-, Transformer-, and state-space baselines. Evaluation on LiTS2017 without dataset-specific fine-tuning yielded a tumour Dice score of 89.84%, providing preliminary evidence of cross-dataset generalisation. Conclusions: Qualitative feature visualisations show that adaptive windowing enhances tumour representation and boundary delineation, demonstrating the effectiveness and interpretability of BCIW-Net for HCC segmentation.

papers.abstract: Melanoma is the most aggressive and rapidly metastasizing malignant neoplasm of the skin and mucous membranes, arising from melanocytes of neuroectodermal origin. Despite substantial advances in immune checkpoint inhibitors and targeted therapy, a significant proportion of patients develop primary or acquired resistance, which is largely attributable to the complex interactions between tumor cells and the tumor microenvironment (TME). This review presents a comprehensive analysis of the cellular and molecular components of the melanoma TME and their contribution to immunosuppression, tumor progression, and therapeutic resistance. The role of keratinocytes as the primary niche-forming cells in the epidermis is examined, including their reprogramming during melanomagenesis and their involvement in drug resistance. Particular attention is given to cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), which orchestrate stromal remodeling, promote immune exclusion, and limit the efficacy of immunotherapy. The phenotypic and functional heterogeneity of innate and adaptive immune cells-macrophages, granulocytes, natural killer cells, dendritic cells, T and B lymphocytes-is discussed in the context of their dual role in antitumor immunity and immune escape. A detailed analysis of immune editing mechanisms, including defective antigen recognition, resistance to apoptosis, and the establishment of an immunosuppressive microenvironment, is provided. The review further summarizes the current landscape of cellular immunotherapy for melanoma. Clinically established approaches, including tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) and CAR-T cells, are discussed with reference to completed phase II-III clinical trials, whereas emerging strategies such as CAR-macrophages and dendritic cell vaccines are presented as largely preclinical or early-phase investigational platforms. It is concluded that the melanoma TME functions as a unified immunosuppressive network rather than a collection of individual cell populations. Based on currently available comparative clinical evidence, reprogramming this network through the combination of cellular platforms with immune checkpoint inhibitors, stromal modulators, and macrophage-repolarizing agents, supported by personalized assessment of TME composition, represents a rational and actively investigated therapeutic direction.

papers.abstract: Stage III/N2 non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) can often be treated with either surgery-based multimodality therapy or definitive chemoradiotherapy. Historical randomized trials showed that surgery improved local control without demonstrating an overall-survival benefit; neither platform demonstrated superiority, although none was designed to establish equivalence. In the immunotherapy era, both pathways have improved through separate evidence streams: perioperative trials compared immunotherapy with chemotherapy-based surgical controls, and PACIFIC compared durvalumab with placebo after chemoradiotherapy. Neither stream determines which complete modern pathway is better for a patient eligible for both, and cross-trial comparisons are confounded by differences in populations, randomization points, and endpoint definitions. This review distinguishes three questions that are often conflated: whether direct comparative evidence exists, how large any relative treatment effect may be, and whether sufficient clinical equipoise exists to justify randomization. Technical resectability, physiological operability, and irradiability define eligibility for a platform, not comparative benefit, and no current biomarker has been shown to modify the relative effect of the two platforms. Comparative uncertainty is most visible in multistation, bulky, or anatomically complex N2 disease, the most practicable starting point for randomization; superiority of either platform, however, has not been demonstrated at either end of the N2 spectrum. A staged randomized comparison of the complete modern pathways, with prespecified analyses of candidate treatment-effect modifiers, is proposed as a reasoned research strategy.

papers.abstract: Neoadjuvant treatment has become an integral component of multidisciplinary management for resectable esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). Over recent decades, treatment has evolved from surgery alone to postoperative chemotherapy, neoadjuvant chemotherapy, intensified systemic therapy, neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, and, more recently, the incorporation of immune checkpoint inhibitors into curative-intent treatment. This evolution has been driven by persistent challenges including systemic recurrence, locoregional failure, treatment-related toxicity, and heterogeneous treatment response. This review traces the evolution of neoadjuvant treatment for resectable ESCC through landmark clinical trials that have shaped current practice. We discuss the transition from postoperative to neoadjuvant chemotherapy, the development of intensified chemotherapy and neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, and the emergence of immunotherapy, distinguishing the established role of adjuvant nivolumab from the emerging role of neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy. We then examine the unresolved relative roles of these strategies and the challenges in treatment selection. Finally, we discuss future directions centered on accurate response assessment, circulating tumor DNA-based molecular residual disease assessment, and response-adapted treatment, with particular emphasis on organ-preserving strategies after a clinical complete response. Although active surveillance has emerged as a potential alternative to immediate surgery in carefully selected patients, accurate identification of residual disease and appropriate surveillance remain essential. Future advances may therefore shift the focus from treatment intensification alone toward response-adapted strategies that can maintain oncological safety while potentially enabling organ preservation.

papers.abstract: Gliomas are the most common brain tumours in children, adolescents, and young adults. In children, paediatric-type low-grade gliomas (pLGG) predominate, while IDH-mutant low-grade gliomas (LGG) become more common in young adulthood. While outcomes with complete surgical resection are excellent, many pLGG patients with residual or unresectable tumours experience significant long-term functional impairment despite conventional medical treatment. IDH-mutant LGG have an unfavourable natural history, with high risk of malignant transformation. With the emergence of precision medicine, targeted therapies have offered hope as more effective treatments. For pLGG, favourable short-term outcomes have been demonstrated with MAPK inhibitors. Significant challenges remain, however, including designing treatment regimens that prevent regrowth, understanding mechanisms and biomarkers of response and resistance, and addressing treatment-related toxicities. Furthermore, pLGG manifest as a chronic disease, and it remains unclear whether targeted therapies can yield superior long-term functional outcomes relative to conventional chemotherapy. For IDH-mutant LGG, IDH inhibitors hold promise; however, it is unknown whether monotherapy will avert malignant transformation. Notably, adolescent and young adult patients have been excluded from many clinical trials, resulting in limited data on the efficacy and toxicity of pLGG-directed targeted therapies in this population. Clinical trials and patient care for LGG should be designed around tumour biology rather than patient age. Overall, the molecular era has transformed our understanding of LGG and facilitated the development of novel therapies. The next challenge is to translate new biological insights into patient- and tumour-specific treatment regimens that can improve long-term disease control and functional outcomes.

papers.abstract: Active surveillance (AS) is the preferred management strategy for localized low-risk prostate cancer. However, clinical debate persists regarding long-term oncologic safety beyond 10 years, the diagnostic reliability and false-negative risk of serial multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) for biopsy deferral, and the prognostic magnitude of adverse pathological patterns such as invasive cribriform morphology. This study aimed to provide a comprehensive meta-analytic synthesis of long-term oncologic survival, dynamic imaging performance, multivariable progression predictors, and longitudinal patient-reported functional outcomes. Registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261479059) and conducted per PRISMA 2020 and GRADE guidelines, electronic searches were performed across PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and Cochrane CENTRAL through January 2026. Twenty-nine prospective cohorts, randomized trials, and diagnostic imaging studies comprising 46,318 patients were included. Time-to-event survival outcomes were synthesized using Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) and random-effects inverse-variance models (REML). Diagnostic accuracy of serial mpMRI was modeled via bivariate random-effects meta-analysis (Reitsma approach). Multivariable-adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) and longitudinal EPIC-26 domain scores were quantitatively pooled. Across 10 cohorts reporting long-term outcomes (N = 24,987), pooled 10-year prostate cancer-specific survival (PCSS) was 98.9% (95% CI: 98.4-99.4%), demonstrating comparable oncologic efficacy to radical therapy. Pooled 10-year metastasis-free survival (MFS) was 96.2% (95% CI: 94.7-97.4%), and 10-year treatment-free survival (TFS) was 54.2% (95% CI: 48.1-60.3%; 95% prediction interval: 31.4-75.8%; I2 = 88.1%). Serial mpMRI demonstrated a pooled sensitivity of 85.6% (95% CI: 74.2-92.6%) and a negative predictive value of 93.4% (95% CI: 89.1-96.3%) for PRECISE 1-3, supporting selective biopsy deferral while recognizing a 6.6% residual risk of missed occult high-grade disease. Invasive cribriform morphology in Grade Group 2 was the strongest independent multivariable predictor of progression (aHR: 12.67, 95% CI: 4.77-33.64; two studies, 1420 patients, 184 progression events). AS preserved baseline urinary continence (+3.0 points at 12 months) and sexual function (-2.0 points at 12 months) compared to profound declines observed after radical prostatectomy (-17.0 and -35.0 points, respectively). Active surveillance provides comparable 10-year oncologic safety to immediate radical therapy while robustly preserving quality of life. Sequential mpMRI facilitates selective biopsy deferral, though invasive cribriform histology and visible target lesions indicate aggressive disease phenotypes that require proactive definitive intervention.

papers.abstract: T-cell-engaging therapies have revolutionized care for relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma. Transformed follicular lymphoma (tFL) has had limited representation in CAR-T or bispecific antibody trials. Thus, outcomes in this subgroup are not well-described. Furthermore, trials that include aggressive disease transformed from indolent lymphomas often report collective outcomes rather than results for individual histologic subsets despite biologic heterogeneity; this limits interpretability of results. Despite these limitations, there are consistent signals that tFL responds well to T-cell-engaging therapies. tFL has a unique tumor microenvironment, but it is not clear if or how this contributes to the favorable outcomes. More robust data are available for CAR-T compared to bispecifics in this population and differences in responsiveness between the two therapies are difficult to ascertain. More research is needed to better understand biologic interaction of tFL with T-cell-engaging therapies and response to therapy to inform future clinical trials.

papers.title: Navigating T-Cell-Directed Therapies in Transformed Follicular Lymphoma.

papers.abstract: Clonal hematopoiesis (CH) is characterized by the proliferation of blood cell clones that possess acquired genetic modifications. While therapy-related CH refers to CH detected in the setting of prior or current treatment in cancer populations, therapy-selected CH demands demonstration that treatment preferentially expanded or maintained an extant clone; therapy-induced CH requires evidence of de novo treatment-associated mutation supported by serial sampling and mutational-signature analyses. To map evidence distinguishing therapy-related, therapy-selected and therapy-induced CH across cancer treatment, including clonal dynamics, genomic features, clinical outcomes and surveillance gaps. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidance, PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, Cochrane Library and Google Scholar were searched from inception through 1 June 2026, and updated on 15 September 2026. Primary evidence mapping was limited to original human studies. Reviews and conceptual sources were used only for context or reference tracking and were ineligible for the primary evidence map. Narrative synthesis was employed as critical variation existed in sequencing platforms, variant allele frequency thresholds, timepoints of sampling, filtering strategies, and outcome definitions. Of 684 records identified, 213 duplicates were removed and 471 records were screened. Across both pathways, 121 full texts were assessed, 87 excluded and 34 primary reports mapped; contextual citations were outside the included set. Contextual references were used for definitions and interpretation and were excluded from the included-report count. Six domains were deductively established and inductively refined during charting: terminology; therapy-associated mechanisms of clonal selection/expansion; genomic architecture; longitudinal clonal dynamics; clinical consequences; and study design and methodological heterogeneity. Treatment-associated selection or expansion of pre-existing TP53 and PPM1D clones was the most consistently reported mechanism of therapy-related CH, while CHEK2 was inconsistently detected. Pediatric cohorts and mutational-signature analyses also supported de novo mutagenesis with therapy in select contexts. Progression to therapy-related myeloid neoplasm was the most consistent outcome across studies; however, cytopenia, CAR-T-therapy-associated toxicity, cardiovascular events and mortality were inconsistently reported. Current evidence supports a spectrum of mechanisms ranging from selection of pre-existing clones to therapy-induced de novo mutation. Existing literature cannot support universal CH screening recommendations or guide treatment decisions. Prospective serial analyses harmonized on definition, employing sensitive baseline assays with paired germline controls and tumor-contamination checks, are needed to justify clinical implementation and assessment of fixed outcomes.

papers.abstract: Peripheral T-cell lymphomas (PTCL) comprise a biologically diverse and clinically aggressive family of mature T/NK-cell neoplasms, for which outcomes remain poor in the majority of patients treated with conventional anthracycline-based frontline regimens. Contemporary classifications (WHO-HAEM5 and ICC) increasingly incorporate immunophenotypic and molecular information, underscoring that "PTCL-NOS" is not a single disease but rather a diagnostic umbrella that includes biologically distinct entities and molecular subgroups. Among these are the TBX21- and GATA3-driven PTCL-NOS subsets, the latter associated with inferior survival and a distinctive cytokine/microenvironmental program. These advances, many of which were shaped by long-standing contributions from the Bologna group, support a rational shift from empiric chemotherapy toward mechanism-based and immune-based interventions. CAR-engineered cellular therapies have revolutionized the care of B-cell malignancies, yet translation to PTCL has been delayed by lineage-specific barriers: (i) fratricide during manufacturing when targeting shared T-cell antigens (e.g., CD5, CD7), (ii) the risk of profound and prolonged T-cell aplasia (a markedly less "replaceable" toxicity than B-cell aplasia), and (iii) product contamination by malignant T-cells in autologous platforms. Recent progress in genome editing (CRISPR/Cas9 and base editing), intracellular antigen "blocking" strategies, and alternative effectors (allogeneic "universal" CAR-T, CAR-NK, and iPSC-derived platforms) has begun to address these obstacles at the manufacturing level, while their downstream clinical consequences (e.g., prolonged cytopenias, infectious risk and delayed immune reconstitution) remain incompletely resolved. Early-phase clinical trials now demonstrate clinically meaningful responses for select targets, particularly CD7, CD5, TRBC1 and CD30, for the pan-T targets. However, the strongest efficacy data remain largely derived from T-cell lymphoblastic malignancies (T-ALL/T-LBL), whereas evidence in mature PTCL remains limited and at an earlier stage, with target-specific differences in safety, immune reconstitution and relapse patterns. This review synthesizes the biological rationale for antigen selection in PTCL, the emerging clinical evidence for leading CAR targets, and the engineering strategies most likely to improve the therapeutic index. It also proposes an integrated hematology perspective on how CAR-based therapies might be positioned relative to transplant and evolving targeted agents in relapsed/refractory PTCL.

papers.abstract: Head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (HNSCCs) are challenging pathologies to treat with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), as only a minority of patients achieve durable clinical benefit. The highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), the frequent loss of antigen presentation, the marked spatial heterogeneity, and the anatomical proximity of tumors to critical structures limit the efficacy and safety of current immunotherapeutic approaches. Immune cell engagers (ICEs) have emerged as promising strategies to redirect endogenous immune cells toward tumor targets. While conventional surface-antigen-directed engagers can bypass major histocompatibility complex (MHC)-restricted antigen presentation, peptide-HLA-directed constructs remain dependent on antigen processing, peptide presentation, and the appropriate HLA allele. More recently, tumor-restricted activation technologies, collectively referred to as "masking immunotherapy", have been developed to preferentially restore target and/or immune-cell engagement under TME-associated conditions, such as increased protease activity. These approaches have demonstrated enhanced tumor-preferential activity and/or improved tolerability in preclinical models; however, the extent to which these properties translate into clinically meaningful tumor selectivity and an improved therapeutic index remains under investigation. In this review, based on the authors' comprehensive literature knowledge and targeted searches, we critically examine the biological rationale, the engineering principles, the current preclinical evidence, and the early clinical development of ICEs with particular emphasis on their potential application in HNSCC. While early clinical studies have demonstrated acceptable safety profiles, clinical activity has generally been poor. We discuss the major barriers that limit clinical translation and we highlight emerging strategies aimed at overcoming these limitations. We believe that successful clinical development of ICEs in HNSCC will likely depend not only on the identification of optimal target antigens, but also on spatially controlled immune activation, integration with TME-modulating approaches, and incorporation of dynamic biomarkers into future clinical trial design.

papers.abstract: Mitigating on-target off-tumor toxicity remains a central challenge for chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy for solid tumors. We developed a hypoxia-inducible CAR-T-cell product targeting carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) that restricts CAR activation to hypoxic tumor niches via oxygen-dependent expression control. In this first-in-human, phase I trial enrolling heavily pretreated patients with relapsed stage IV non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), a single infusion of the investigational product achieved an objective response rate of 47% and a disease control rate of 87%, with a manageable safety profile. Exploratory analyses showed that clinical outcomes were associated with baseline factors. Deep single-cell profiling indicated that the clinical response was associated with the expansion of hypoxia-adapted, tumor-reactive-like CD8+ T cells alongside coordinated functional maturation of natural killer (NK) cells. Collectively, these data provide clinical proof-of-concept for hypoxia-inducible CAR design and inform the rational development of strategies leveraging tumor microenvironmental features in solid tumor cellular immunotherapy.

papers.abstract: The basal ganglia's (BG) contribution to motor control is thought to involve invigorating movement based on environmental constraints, yet this has primarily been studied in the limb system. We hypothesized that the BG similarly regulate the respiratory and articulatory systems during speech. We recorded local field potentials and single-unit activity from the subthalamic nucleus (STN) and globus pallidus (GP) in humans during a speech task where the Lombard Effect was used to modulate environmental constraints. GP and STN exhibited distinct temporal profiles during speech production. Neither region robustly encoded produced speech intensity. Instead, neural populations tracked ambient background noise levels, even during baseline, with high decoding accuracy. The ambient-noise-modulated sites were an independent population from speech-modulated sites. We theorize that the code is leveraged in downstream BG-cortical loop nodes to invigorate speech oro-motor gestures and co-speech manual limb gestures, both of which respond to ambient noise levels to maintain high-fidelity communication.

papers.abstract: Diverse chemicals biosynthesis demand distinct precursor acetyl-CoA and energy inputs, yet strategies balancing carbon atom economy and energy generation for varied products remain scarce. Here, we design an autonomous hybrid energy-carbon balancing apparatus (ATHENA) to establish a paradigm for redox-driven, dynamically adaptive regulation of carbon conservation and energy synthesis in Escherichia coli. ATHENA features modularization of acetyl-CoA and NADH synthesis pathways for carbon conservation and energy generation, paired with NADH-responsive positive and negative genetic circuits constructed using the BsRex sensor and antisense RNA. This system enables intracellular redox state-dependent rational metabolic flux allocation to balance carbon atom economy and energy generation. Ultimately, ATHENA significantly improves yields and titers of five products with differential acetyl-CoA and energy demands. In the 5-L bioreactor, acetate yield markedly exceeds its native theoretical yield, while that of mevalonate nearly approaches this theoretical upper limit. This work provides a universal strategy for constructing high carbon-yield microbial chassis cells.

papers.abstract: Environmental genomics has transformed our view of the microbial world, yet progress remains largely prokaryote-centric. Among microbial eukaryotes, inconsistent marker choice and limited species-level resolution blunt diversity estimates and hinder cross-study synthesis. Consequently, regional‑to‑global gradients in richness, turnover, and phylogenetic structure remain poorly resolved. Here we establish a global mitogenome-based framework that converts shotgun metagenomes into species‑resolved, phylogeny‑anchored inventories. From 3,400 metagenomes spanning 362 lakes on seven continents, we reconstruct ~20,000 mitochondrial metagenome-assembled genomes (mitoMAGs), densely populating previously sparse branches of the eukaryotic tree-notably SAR (Stramenopiles-Alveolata-Rhizaria), Cryptophyceae, and Haptista. An empirically calibrated 98.1% mitoMAG‑identity threshold delineates species and tethers community profiles to an evolutionary backbone. On this backbone, coverage‑standardized inventories recover canonical ecological patterns: mesotrophic richness peaks, surface-layer expansion of phylogenetic breadth, and spring maxima with the strongest surface-deep coupling at vernal mixing; supporting the framework. Treating mitoMAGs as primer‑free barcodes yields a single, species‑level, phylogeny‑aware currency that renders richness, evenness, and phylogenetic breadth directly comparable across datasets, depths, seasons, and regions. By placing microbial eukaryotes on an analytical footing comparable to prokaryotes, the resulting atlas brings their diversity into reach and lays the groundwork for future high-throughput, species-aware monitoring and ecological forecasting.

papers.abstract: Semiconductor zinc oxide (ZnO) nanostructures as classic photonic materials have sparked the development of low-cost, high-performance fluorescence sensors; however, their scalable clinical applications remain hampered by inadequate sensitivity. Here, we engineer a high-curvature photo-heterostructure aggregate-enhanced fluorescence (PAEF) sensor based on bubble-scaffolded ZnO nanorods. Leveraging synergistic evanescent field coupling and self-aggregation of photo-heterostructures, PAEF sensor streamlines efficient isolation (~90%) and ultrasensitive profiling of tumor extracellular vesicles (EVs) in a single assay, achieving sensitivity <10 EVs/μL (104-fold better than ELISA) without additional amplification, outperforming most state-of-the-art EV fluorescence assays. This self-sufficient sensor enables accurate monitoring of targeted therapeutic efficacy in mouse xenograft models via simultaneous dual-marker readout. We further show its clinical utility in hepatocellular carcinoma diagnosis with ≥96% accuracy (≥98% specificity) in two cohorts (n = 146), improving dynamic monitoring of surgical treatment responses, particularly in alpha-fetoprotein-negative patients. This work provides a cost-effective ultrasensitive liquid biopsy tool advancing non-invasive cancer diagnosis.

papers.abstract: Sleep problems are common among cancer survivors and are linked to poorer quality of life. In the general United States (US) population, socioeconomic status (SES) is strongly associated with sleep health, but emerging evidence suggests that these benefits may be diminished among non-White racial/ethnic groups. Whether such patterns extend to cancer survivors is unknown. We analyzed data on 25,732 adult cancer survivors from National Health Interview Surveys. Sleep duration (normal 6-8 h; short ≤ 5 h; long ≥ 9 h) and troubled sleep (≥ 3 days/week of difficulty falling or staying asleep) were assessed via self-report. SES indicators included educational attainment and family income. Poisson regression models with race/ethnicity-by-SES interaction terms were used to estimate racial/ethnic differences in SES-sleep associations. Among non-Hispanic (NH) White survivors, higher education and income were consistently associated with lower prevalence of short sleep and troubled sleep. These SES gradients were muted or reversed among NH Black and Hispanic survivors. For example, NH White survivors with a bachelor's degree had substantially lower odds of short sleep compared with those with ≤ high school education, whereas no such association was observed among NH Black or Hispanic survivors. When stratifying by both education and income, income showed more consistent associations with sleep across all groups, while additional benefits of higher education were observed only among NH White survivors. SES-sleep gradients differ markedly across racial/ethnic groups among US cancer survivors. Tailored interventions addressing structural and socioeconomic inequities may be needed to improve sleep health and reduce disparities in survivorship.

papers.abstract: The International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) staging system for advanced ovarian cancer has remained largely static since 2014, with stage IV subdivided into IVA and IVB without further stratification. Emerging evidence suggests substantial prognostic heterogeneity within stage IV, yet large-scale validation remains limited. We analyzed 28,010 patients from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database (2010-2022) and 1175 from the Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center (SYSUCC) (2010-2026). Propensity score matching (1:1) balanced baseline characteristics. Overall survival (OS) was compared across subgroups. We defined IVA-T1a as patients meeting FIGO IVA criteria with intra-abdominal disease limited to one ovary (intact capsule). We defined IVB-ILNT2 as stage IVB with metastasis confined to a single extra-abdominal lymph node station and intra-abdominal disease ≤ T2. IVB patients were stratified by metastatic pattern and surgical outcome. In SEER, IVA-T1a patients (n = 49) showed no OS difference versus stage II (HR 1.08, 95% CI: 0.95-1.23, p = 0.250), but significantly better survival than stage IIIA (HR 1.35, 95% CI: 1.08-1.62, p = 0.024). Findings were validated in SYSUCC (IVA-T1a n = 15; vs. stage II p = 0.638, vs. IIIA p = 0.026). Among IVB patients, those with single-station lymph node metastases achieving R0/R1 resection (n = 152) had median OS of 29.0 months, comparable to stage IIIC patients (HR 1.08, p = 0.872). In SYSUCC, IVB-ILNT2 subgroup (n = 65) demonstrated survival comparable to stage II (p = 4e-04 vs. other IVB) and significantly better than stage IIIA. These findings suggest that such patients may have a more favorable prognosis than implied by their current stage designation and underscore the need for prospective validation to determine whether treatment de-escalation could be considered in these specific subsets without compromising outcomes. Future FIGO revisions should consider refined classification incorporating intra-abdominal tumor burden and metastatic pattern, pending consistent validation across multiple independent populations.

papers.abstract: Rurality is one of many disparities leading to lower cancer screening rates, as well as higher cancer incidence and mortality. Our study was designed to evaluate rural-urban disparities in incidence and cancer-specific mortality for the leading cancers in the State of Michigan from January 1, 2017, through December 31, 2021. Data was obtained for the 10 leading cancers in both incidence and cancer-specific mortality from the Michigan Department of Health and Human Service. Rural-urban comparisons were made for incidence, incidence by SEER stage, and cancer-specific mortality and reported as rate ratios. Combining the 10 leading cancers in Michigan during our study period, the age-adjusted incidence rate was significantly lower (IRR 0.95, 95% CI 0.94-0.96, p < 0.001), whereas the age-adjusted cancer-specific mortality rate was significantly higher (MRR 1.05, 95% CI 1.03-1.07, p = 0.023) in our rural study population. Regarding cancers with proven screening benefits, age-adjusted incidence rates and cancer-specific mortality rates for female breast (IRR 0.87; 95% CI 0.85-0.89; p < 0.001 and MRR 0.87; 95% CI 0.81-0.98; p = 0.012) and prostate (IRR 0.86; 95% CI 0.83-0.88; p < 0.001 and MRR 0.92; 95% CI 0.86-0.98; p = 0.012) cancer were significantly lower in rural Michigan. Lung and bronchus cancer had significantly higher age-adjusted incidence rates and cancer-specific mortality rates in our rural study population (IRR 1.07; 95% CI 1.05-1.10; p < 0.001 and MRR 1.17; 95% CI 1.14-1.20; p < 0.001). Our rural Michigan population had significantly lower incidence rates for the 10 leading cancers in incidence, female breast cancer, and prostate cancer in our study period. However, rurality was associated with higher age-adjusted cancer-specific mortality for the 10 leading cancers regarding mortality and for lung and bronchus cancer. Continued focus on Michigan's existing public health programs may further bridge rural disparity gaps.

papers.abstract: Radioresistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a coordinated adaptive state rather than failure of a single pathway, sustained by reinforced redox buffering and suppressed immune activation. Strategies that intensify radiation damage without disrupting this state have shown limited efficacy. We sought to determine whether radiosensitization can be achieved by destabilizing tumor oxidative homeostasis while restoring immune competence. A BSA-templated Fe/Mn nanoassembly incorporating the thiol-reactive agent RRX-001 and folate targeting (BFMR-FA) was developed as a multifunctional and MRI-visible platform. Its biological effects were evaluated across radioresistant cellular systems, organoids, and orthotopic tumor models. BFMR-FA shifts the redox equilibrium of tumor cells beyond a recoverable threshold. By depleting glutathione and suppressing the SLC7A11-GPX4 axis, it converts radiation-induced oxidative stress from a transient signal into sustained lipid peroxidation, resulting in convergent ferroptotic and apoptotic cell death. This transition is accompanied by the emergence of immunogenic stress signals and activation of the STING-TBK1-IRF3 pathway, enabling dendritic cell maturation and expansion of cytotoxic T-cell responses. In vivo, these effects translate into near-complete suppression of radioresistant tumor growth with systemic tolerance. The Fe/Mn composition enables direct visualization of intratumoral delivery by T1-weighted MRI. These findings support a model in which radiosensitization is achieved not by amplifying tumor damage alone, but by collapsing the adaptive redox state that constrains it. The resulting oxidative destabilization coupled with immune activation defines an oxidative homeostasis collapse-driven radio-immuno synergy, providing a generalizable framework for overcoming therapeutic resistance in solid tumors.

papers.abstract: The role of small extracellular vesicles (sEVs), such as exosomes, in cell-to-cell communication is increasingly recognized. Both during development and postnatally, sEVs have been shown to mediate a multitude of essential functions in the central nervous system. While abnormal sEV biogenesis has been observed in a number of neurodevelopmental disorders, a causal link has been largely lacking. We clinically evaluated five families in which newborns presented with a novel neonatal-onset encephalopathy. Positional mapping, exome sequencing, and trio exome sequencing were utilized to identify the underlying genetic variants. Additionally, we utilized Vps25 hypomorphic mouse mutants and performed cellular assays to evaluate ESCRT-II interaction, cellular localization, and sEV secretion and cargo capacities. The observed lethal encephalopathy is characterized by severe hypotonia, brain anomalies, and epilepsy. In families 1, 4, and 5 (multiplex consanguineous), we identified a novel homozygous missense variant in VPS25 as the likely candidate. Family 2 comprises a simplex case with two missense variants in trans in VPS25, one of which impacts the same residue as in the other three families. Family 3 also comprises a simplex case where we revealed a homozygous missense variant. VPS25 is an essential component of ESCRT-II, itself required for sEV biogenesis. We show that Vps25 hypomorphic mouse mutants recapitulate the developmental brain malformation observed in patients. We also show that mutant VPS25 is associated with abnormal ESCRT-II interaction, abnormal cellular localization, and highly abnormal sEVs. Specifically, mutant cells displayed engorged multivesicular bodies and were significantly defective in their capacity to secrete sEVs such as exosomes, while secreted sEVs contained altered cargo, lacking vital proteins for axon protection and maintenance. We report a novel neurodevelopmental disorder caused by biallelic hypomorphic variants in VPS25. The consistent impact of these variants on sEV biogenesis suggests a potential pathomechanism. While future cases will further delineate the phenotypic spectrum, these findings offer a new perspective on abnormal sEVs as drivers of human neurodevelopmental disorders.

papers.abstract: Climate change is transforming living systems worldwide, with its impact primarily mediated through organisms' metabolic rates. Understanding how metabolic rate responds to climate change and identifying which ecosystems and geographic areas will be severely affected remain urgent priorities. Here, we assemble and meta-analyse a dataset to establish the current state of knowledge on thermal sensitivity of metabolic rate (i.e. the degree of metabolic response to temperature) and its plasticity, and how these vary geographically and across ecosystems in invertebrates-Earth's most diverse yet understudied organisms. We demonstrate that invertebrates from aquatic ecosystems exhibit a lower metabolic response to temperature than those from terrestrial ones, with this response increasing with latitude, though more sharply in terrestrial ecosystems. Organisms inhabiting warm and stable climates show greater capacity for metabolic plasticity to counteract temperature effects. Conversely, cold and more variable climates shape heightened thermal sensitivity, particularly in terrestrial ecosystems. We forecast substantial increases in metabolic rates even under a modest climate change scenario (CMIP5-RCP2.6), with increases of up to 26.6% in aquatic and 43.9% in terrestrial invertebrates. These pronounced warming impacts on terrestrial species and those at higher latitudes suggest that they are among the most at risk, more so than previously thought.

papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease involves progressive α-synuclein pathology, but how this reshapes the brain's spatial immunometabolic landscape, and how oligodendrocytes participate, remain incompletely defined. Here we combine single-nucleus RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics and spatial metabolomics in male A53T α-synuclein transgenic mice across disease stages, together with male mice carrying adeno-associated virus-mediated α-synuclein overexpression, human midbrain and cerebrospinal fluid samples. We describe a disease-associated oligodendrocyte lineage marked by elevated Il33 and Kirrel3 that expands with pathology in both mouse models. Interleukin 33 is upregulated in oligodendrocytes and its receptor ST2 in microglia, and bidirectional manipulation of oligodendrocyte Il33 alters microglial ST2 activation, insoluble α-synuclein burden and motor performance. In the substantia nigra and ventral tegmental area, transcriptomic and metabolomic changes converge on lipid- and glutamate-related pathways. Both proteins are also elevated in human Parkinson's disease midbrain and cerebrospinal fluid. These data implicate oligodendrocyte interleukin 33-ST2 signalling and provide a spatially resolved resource.

papers.abstract: Although diphtheria toxin-like ADP-ribosyltransferases (ARTDs) are implicated in host-virus interactions, the specific antiviral mechanisms of certain family members remain largely undefined. Here, we reveal that mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase PARP10 restricts viral replication by forming biomolecular condensates via multivalent interactions among its structured domains. PARP10 condensates enhance enzymatic activity, resulting in increased NAD⁺ consumption that ultimately inhibits viral replication. The antiviral effects of PARP10 are shown to require both its catalytic activity and NAD⁺ regulation, as catalytic mutants and PARP10 inhibitors abrogate these effects, while reduction of NAD⁺ potently restricts viral replication. Furthermore, we identify auto-ADP-ribosylation as an intrinsic negative feedback mechanism modulating PARP10 condensation. These findings establish PARP10 condensation as a compartmentalization strategy that amplifies local NAD⁺ consumption to safeguard host antiviral immunity.
